title: Ceramide synthesis mediates colorectal cancer metastasis through a YAP-driven regenerative program.
data_url: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE286166 (plus GSE286167, GSE286168, GSE286169, GSE285872, GSE285873; BioProject PRJNA1208038)

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Found six public GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus) series the paper did not list in any index I could reach, by searching GEO for the preprint-style title 'revival stemness program'. Downloaded and parsed all four bulk RNA-sequencing count matrices (GSE286166/167/168/169, 1.4M/829K/890K/1.1M gzipped). Each has 54,353 unique mouse Ensembl gene IDs; sample columns number 34, 23, 18 and 35 (110 total), exactly matching the GEO sample counts. No missing values, no duplicate gene IDs. Library sizes range 25,458 to 12.8M counts (one near-empty sample in GSE286167). Pulled per-sample metadata for all six series and tabulated group sizes. Listed file sizes for the two large series: GSE285872 (assay of transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing, 12 samples) is a 1.6 GB tar, GSE285873 (single-cell RNA sequencing, 10 samples) a 395 MB tar; both over the 50 MB cap, so metadata only.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Almost everything about the biology. The paper is not open access: Europe PMC has no PMCID, no full text, no supplement, and the publisher page returns HTTP 403, so I never saw the data availability statement, the methods, or any supplementary table. The abstract is the only paper text I read. The link between this paper and these GEO series rests on matching title wording, the Yilmaz/Zhang/Goswami author list in the GEO contributor fields, and matching experimental design (Degs1 knockout, short-hairpin YAP knockdown, high-fat diet, Basp1-GFP reporter sorting, palmitic acid, carmofur).

a1_downloadable.note: Verified by download, not by reading. All six GEO series are public with no login or access application; I fetched and parsed the four bulk count matrices directly from the NCBI FTP site.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Borderline pass, with a caveat. The only label available is the experimental group (Degs1-knockout vs scrambled, high-fat vs control diet, GFP-positive vs GFP-negative, carmofur vs control), which does sit in GEO's sample characteristics fields. But matrix column names are cryptic lab codes ('239044.intCt', 'X20.4.18.201038.intCt') that do not obviously map to the sample titles, so the join is manual for all 110 samples. Every biologically interesting outcome - liver metastasis burden per mouse, measured ceramide concentrations, YAP nuclear localisation - is in no downloadable file I could find.

a3_inputs_present.note: Verified in the files. Raw integer gene counts are present for all 54,353 genes, with Ensembl mouse gene IDs, gene symbols and gene biotype as columns. No identifier lookups needed.

a4_units_stated.note: Verified in the files. Columns are suffixed '.intCt' (integer counts) and values are non-negative integers; the GEO processing field states Cell Ranger / standard alignment to mouse genome GRCm39. Units are consistent within each matrix.

a5_enough_rows.note: THIS IS THE KILLER, verified by counting columns in the downloaded files. The unit of analysis is the mouse or organoid sample, and there are 110 bulk RNA-sequencing samples total, split across four separate small experiments with 3-12 samples per group, plus 10 single-cell samples and 12 chromatin-accessibility samples. The checklist needs roughly 1,500 labelled rows, or 400 for classification. 110 is short by more than threefold even for the loosest bar, and the real effective n per comparison is about 10. Treating the 54,353 genes as rows would be the wrong unit - genes within a sample are not independent examples.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~4.2 MB gzipped / ~90 MB in memory for all four bulk matrices; the single-cell (395 MB) and chromatin (1.6 GB) tars exceed the 50 MB download cap but were not needed.
a6_fits_laptop.note: Verified: all four bulk matrices loaded into pandas on this laptop without difficulty.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Sample counts in the downloaded matrices (34/23/18/35) match GEO's stated sample counts exactly. One labelling defect: GEO's series titles for GSE286167 and GSE286168 are swapped relative to their contents - GSE286167 is titled '[BulkRNAseq_HFD]' but holds the GFP-sorted Basp1 reporter samples, while GSE286168 is titled '[BulkRNAseq_GFP]' but holds the control-diet/high-fat-diet samples. The per-sample metadata is internally consistent and authoritative. GSE286166's CSV also carries 210 empty padding columns. I could not cross-check against the paper because it is paywalled.

a8_label_provenance.note: The experimental-group label is an assignment the experimenters made at the bench (diet, genetic knockout, drug), not another model's output and not computable from the counts, so no circularity there. Flagged for the record: the paper's headline readout, the 'YAP-driven regenerative' signature score, WOULD be computed from the same expression matrix that would serve as features - using that as a target would be leakage by construction.

honest_claim_h3: Not applicable - no model is viable. The strongest honest claim the deposited data could support is descriptive: 'in 110 mouse colon tumour and organoid samples from one laboratory, blocking the ceramide-making enzyme Degs1 shifts expression of a regeneration gene programme', which is a differential-expression result the paper already reports, not a prediction.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a tumour's gene activity profile to predict whether its fat-driven ceramide pathway is switched on and driving spread.
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered: 110 mouse colon tumour and organoid bulk gene-expression profiles (54,353 genes each) from four perturbation experiments - Degs1 gene knockout, YAP knockdown, high-fat versus control diet, palmitic acid, and the drug carmofur - all verified by opening the files.
plain_idea.predict: Which experimental condition a sample came from, or a continuous ceramide level. The condition comes from the experimenters' own bench assignment recorded in the repository metadata; the ceramide levels were measured by mass spectrometry but were not deposited anywhere I could find.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: If it worked, a cancer lab could read ceramide-pathway activity off a routine expression profile instead of running a lipid mass-spectrometry assay. It does not work here because 110 samples, with about 10 per group, is far too few to train or honestly evaluate anything.

ml_idea: The project considered and rejected: train a classifier or regressor on mouse colon tumour expression profiles to infer ceramide-pathway activity (Degs1 knockout versus intact, high-fat versus control diet, Basp1-high versus Basp1-low). It dies on sample size: 110 bulk samples, 10 single-cell samples, 12 chromatin samples, all mouse, all one laboratory, 3-12 replicates per group. The one target that would have been worth predicting - measured ceramide concentration, or liver metastasis burden per mouse - was never deposited in a public repository; those numbers are in the paywalled Science supplement. A variant project, predicting chromatin accessibility from DNA sequence using the 12-sample chromatin dataset, would reach enough rows by counting peaks, but needs a GPU, exceeds the size budget at 1.6 GB, and competes directly with Enformer, ChromBPNet and AlphaGenome on a task where this paper's biology adds nothing.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, with the download and parse step actually timed: all four matrices fetched and loaded into pandas in under a minute on this laptop. The 4 hours is for hand-mapping 110 cryptic matrix column names onto GEO sample records, which has no shortcut.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the sample columns in the processed matrices. It takes two minutes and returns 110, which is the whole answer. I did this first.

verdict_reason: Fails A5 on sample size, verified by opening the files. The deposited data is 110 bulk RNA-sequencing samples (plus 10 single-cell and 12 chromatin-accessibility samples), all mouse, all from one laboratory, with 3-12 replicates per experimental group - roughly a tenth of what the checklist requires even for classification. The data itself is clean and freely downloadable, and the biology is first-rate, but this is a mechanistic cancer-biology paper whose omics deposits exist to support differential-expression figures, not to train models. Compounding it: the paper is paywalled with no PMCID, so the quantitative measurements that would have made an interesting target - ceramide concentrations by mass spectrometry, liver metastasis burden per mouse - are locked in supplementary tables and were deposited in no repository I could find (Metabolomics Workbench has nothing from this group). The only label present in the files is the experimenters' own group assignment.
